texto:
Amazon is testing a live chat function that lets third-party sellers talk to customers in real time from inside Seller Central, according to a LinkedIn post published today by Will Haire, co-founder of the Amazon and Walmart marketplace agency BellaVix. The feature sits in the Buyer Messages section of the seller interface as a switch labelled "Enable Real-Time Chat," carrying a blue "Beta" badge. Amazon has not published an announcement or a help page about it; PPC Land found none on October 26, and the only evidence so far comes from sellers who say the option has appeared in their own accounts.
In Short
Some Amazon sellers now see a new switch that lets them go "online" and chat with shoppers instantly, instead of answering messages hours later. If it spreads, shoppers with a question about a product could get an answer while they are still deciding whether to buy. Nobody yet knows whether this helps sales, which sellers have it, or how Amazon will judge sellers who switch it on and then miss messages.
What the post shows
Haire's post is short. "Spotted something new in Amazon Seller Central," it begins. "Inside Buyer Messages, there's now a toggle for 'Enable Real-Time Chat' (currently in Beta). When switched on, sellers appear online and can chat with customers in real time."
The post includes an image of the Buyer Messages header bar, with the relevant area outlined in red. In the Amazon interface Haire shared, the switch is set to off, and a status line beneath the label reads "You are now Offline." An information icon next to the label opens a tooltip with a single sentence of description: "Turn this on to appear online and chat with customers in real-time."
The same header bar holds three other controls. To the right of the chat switch sit a "Messaging Settings" drop-down menu, a link to "Manage automated responses," and a "More" menu. The inbox below the bar displays "No messages." Nothing in the interface Haire shared describes eligibility, the marketplaces involved, operating hours, response-time targets or how a buyer starts a live conversation from the customer side.
Haire closed the post with two questions rather than claims: "Does live chat lead to more conversions on pre-purchase questions?" and "Has anyone else seen this on their accounts?" He offered no data on the feature's effect and did not say which marketplace his account operates in.
A second sighting
Haire was not alone. On Sellers Ask Sellers, an independent forum for marketplace merchants, a member posting as Old-Timer reported on October 26 noticing a beta option for real-time chat for buyers, and said they had switched it on. According to that post, the seller already runs a chat window on their own website and expects the Amazon version to be useful for shoppers wanting a quick answer about customising an item. The thread, filed under the forum's customer-messages tag, carried three images labelled as the beta option, its details and the enabled state, and had no replies when PPC Land viewed it.
Two independent reports on the same day suggest a staged rollout rather than a single-account glitch. Neither establishes how many sellers can see the switch.
How Amazon messaging works today
Communication between shoppers and third-party sellers on Amazon has for years run through an asynchronous, email-like system, Buyer-Seller Messaging, which Amazon mediates. Buyers send questions, sellers reply from Seller Central, and Amazon logs and polices the exchange. The system is tightly governed. Sellers cannot use it to solicit reviews, offer compensation for feedback or push buyers to off-Amazon channels, and Amazon controls which message types are allowed.
That control has consequences in other workflows too. When Amazon told US sellers that prepaid return labels would be mandatory on seller-fulfilled orders, the company specified that labels sent through Buyer-Seller Messaging or other channels outside the Manage Returns workflow will not count toward the new seven-day deadline that starts on December 18, 2026. Messaging remains a channel for conversation, not for formal transactions.
Messages are also where friction surfaces. PPC Land reported in April how sellers were handling buyers who threatened negative feedback in messages, with Amazon's anti-manipulation rules barring refunds or compensation offered in exchange for removing a rating. A live channel shortens the distance between that kind of exchange and the seller's screen.
Real-time chat would change the rhythm, not the gatekeeper. Based on the tooltip, the seller's presence is binary: online or offline. The interface shows no queue, no typing indicator and no hours setting, though those may sit inside the "Messaging Settings" menu that the image does not expand.
The response-time question
The post had drawn 12 reactions and 8 comments when PPC Land viewed it. Most commenters were sellers and agency operators, and several focused on risk rather than upside.
Lesley Hensell, who works on getting suspended ecommerce sellers reinstated, raised the question of what happens when a live message goes unanswered. "The real question is what happens when a seller misses a message," she wrote. "Amazon has a habit of turning useful features into performance expectations."
Mudassir Ali, an Amazon brand manager, pointed to the measurement sellers already live with. "Anything that reduces response-time pressure on Buyer Messages helps smaller teams, but I'd still keep an eye on the 24-hour response metric in Account Health, since that's what Amazon weighs," he wrote.
The concern is not abstract. Seller Central's Account Health dashboard already tracks Order Defect Rate, Late Shipment Rate, Cancellation Rate and On-Time Delivery Rate, and sellers' standing depends on those numbers. Whether a live conversation is timed differently from a standard message, and whether a seller who appears online but fails to reply is judged more harshly, is not covered by anything in the post or the tooltip. Amazon has not said.
Kagan Adair, co-founder of Click2Refund and Profit Cyclops, addressed the measurement problem from another direction. "It's worth testing, but keep coverage hours consistent," he wrote. "Otherwise, it's hard to tell whether live chat actually improves conversions."
That is a fair description of the difficulty. A seller who goes online only during quiet hours, or only during peak periods, would struggle to isolate the effect of the chat from the effect of the time of day. Jonny Golding, an ecommerce growth consultant, suggested a direct comparison: "It would be interesting to compare conversion rates on listings with live chat enabled against similar listings without it."
What sellers say they are seeing
Evidence of results is thin. Joshua Mangus, chief executive of RivrHub, wrote the most concrete comment in the thread: "We're testing, not much to report yet."
Others treated the feature as a source of product information rather than a sales lever. Tom C., founder of Eleviam, wrote: "If the same pre purchase question keeps coming up in chat, that's basically a free list of what's missing from your listing." The seller account eSeller World was more tentative: "I wonder if being able to answer buyers instantly will actually help more of them make a purchase. Would be good to see how this works in practice."
Hamza Zahid, an Amazon listing designer, called it an "Interesting update" and wrote that "Faster answers to pre-purchase questions could make a real difference in conversion rates." No commenter supplied figures.
Why it matters for marketers
For brands that sell on Amazon, the conversion rate on a product page determines how far advertising budgets stretch. Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands bids are paid per click, so any change that converts more of those clicks into orders alters the economics of every campaign pointed at that listing. Equally, a live channel that sellers staff poorly could produce the opposite effect if shoppers wait for answers that never arrive.
The test also lands in a period when Amazon is pushing the pre-purchase conversation towards its own AI. Amazon attributed nearly $12 billion in incremental annualized sales to Rufus in 2025, its shopping assistant, which answers product questions by synthesising reviews and listing details. In May, the company merged Rufus and Alexa+ into a single assistant called Alexa for Shopping, citing more than 300 million Rufus users in 2025 and a 60% higher purchase completion rate among engaged shoppers. Research cited in that coverage found Rufus handled 38% of Amazon sessions during Black Friday 2025.
Live seller chat would put a human alternative next to that machine. Which one a shopper sees first, and whether Rufus answers before a seller can, is unknown. The interface Haire shared offers no clue.
Seller Central itself has been changing quickly. Amazon announced at its Accelerate conference in September that Seller Assistant would gain persistent memory and automated workflows, including templates for account health monitoring. Days later, Amazon said it would let US sellers bring eBay, Shopify, TikTok and Walmart orders into Seller Central over the coming months, citing its own figure that more than 95% of independent sellers also sell elsewhere. A live customer channel would add one more task to a dashboard that Amazon is positioning as the seller's main workplace.
Timing matters too. Black Friday falls on November 27, 2026, and Cyber Monday on November 30, with deal submissions for the period having closed on October 20. A beta that appears about a month before the busiest selling period of the year would put live staffing decisions in front of sellers exactly when message volumes rise.
What is not known
The list of open points is longer than the list of facts. The post does not say:
- which marketplaces show the toggle, or whether it is limited to the US store
- what share of sellers have access, and how Amazon chose them
- how buyers see a seller's online status or start a chat
- whether chats are subject to the same content restrictions as Buyer-Seller Messaging
- whether live chats count toward the 24-hour response measurement in Account Health
- whether Amazon plans to report conversion data from the beta to participating sellers
Amazon has not commented publicly. PPC Land found no Seller Central news post or help page describing the feature.

Summary
Who: Amazon's third-party sellers, with the test first described publicly by Will Haire, co-founder of BellaVix, and separately by a seller on the Sellers Ask Sellers forum. Commenters included sellers, agency operators and a reinstatement specialist.
What: An "Enable Real-Time Chat" switch, labelled Beta, has appeared in the Buyer Messages section of Seller Central for some sellers. When turned on, sellers appear online and can chat with customers in real time. Amazon has not published an announcement or help documentation.
When: Both reports were posted on October 26, 2026, about a month before Black Friday on November 27.
Where: Seller Central's Buyer Messages area. The marketplaces covered are not stated.
Why: Live answers to pre-purchase questions could affect conversion rates on listings that brands pay to advertise, while sellers worry that the feature could become another performance expectation tied to Account Health. It also places a human channel next to Rufus and Alexa for Shopping, which Amazon already uses to answer shoppers' questions.
